newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal's central bank sets limits on import finance.
newsitem.headline: Nepal's central bank sets limits on import finance.

text.p: Nepal's central bank has set limits on commercial bank lending to foreign trade companies to check financial irregularities that resulted in a scandal earlier this year, a senior banking official said on Tuesday.
"No bank can open LCs (letters of credit) on behalf of any firm exceeding 20 times its (the firm's) capital," said Bhaikaji Shrestha, a senior manager of the Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB).

Shrestha told Reuters that new NRB rules would require importers to import goods only after opening LCs with valid bank approval and all import documents must be endorsed by banks for clearance by customs authorities.
Earlier, importers could avoid customs checks as bank endorsements of letters of credit were not necessary.

This was misused by many firms to make letters of credit for amounts far exceeding the value of actual imports carried out to circumvent foreign exchange restrictions in the Himalayan kingdom, officials said.
Many LCs had been issued to firms for amounts beyond their financial limits since there was no ceiling fixed, authorities said.

In June, a government-appointed commission accused more than 90 Nepali businessmen of violating state control rules on foreign exchange in 1994 and 1995 by deflecting $36.1 million through fake letters of credit.

Authorities said the scandal, one of the biggest in the country's financial sector, resulted in a customs loss of $9 million because the goods supposed to have been bought with the foreign exchange acquired were not imported.

The report named more than 40 foreign business firms based in Hong Kong, Singapore, Dubai, Taiwan and South Korea whose documents were produced by Nepali businessmen to obtain payment without actually importing any goods.
Commercial banks were earlier asked not to issue letters of credit to 40 foreign firms named in the report and to withhold outstanding payments to these firms.
So far, 15 Nepali businessmen including two top executives, have been arrested and produced in court in connection with the scandal.
